decor: Vintage Art Déco illustration in a museum catalog style, the same visual language as the rest of the game: elegant sepia ink line-art over RICH, SATURATED watercolour washes on warm cream parchment — deep forest and olive greens, warm honeyed wood, burnished brass and copper, terracotta and ochre accents, dusty rose and soft teal on the fabrics, all laid down with real pigment density and clear tonal contrast between light and shadow. The colour is full-bodied and inviting, never pale, never washed out, never a faded pastel — think a beautifully printed vintage travel poster rather than a bleached old photograph. Subtle paper grain across the whole image, warm directional morning light with defined shadows. PORTRAIT 9:16 vertical canvas, filled entirely by a single full-bleed illustration that runs to the very pixel edge on all four sides. No text, no watermark, no UI element. SUBJECT: a first-person view from BEHIND a flea-market stall, as seen by the stallholder standing right up against their own table. The camera stands DIRECTLY BEHIND the stall, squarely facing it, exactly where the stallholder stands — a strict head-on, symmetrical, one-point perspective, centred on the middle of the table. The table is seen FRONT ON: its near edge and its far edge are both straight HORIZONTAL lines, parallel to each other and parallel to the bottom of the canvas, each running the full width of the frame from left edge to right edge. The table is never turned at an angle, never seen from the corner, never diagonal, never in three-quarter view. The camera is at the eye level of a person standing at the table — a head higher than the table top — and is tilted gently downwards, so that the cloth-covered table top is comfortably visible as a broad surface receding away from the viewer. It is a mild downward tilt, the natural angle of someone glancing at their own goods, not a steep overhead view. There is exactly ONE table in the foreground: a single trestle table, and no other table, plank, shelf or counter anywhere in the lower half of the picture. It is LONGER THAN THE FRAME and runs off both the left and the right edges of the canvas: neither of its ends is visible, its far edge reads as one straight horizontal line crossing the entire width from edge to edge, and it must look like a continuous counter spanning the whole bottom of the screen. Its faded green-and-cream striped cloth covers the whole table top in one continuous piece, from the near edge right up to the far edge, so the eye reads one unbroken cloth surface — no bare wood plank across it, no gap, and no ground or cobblestones visible anywhere between the near edge and the far edge. The camera is RIGHT UP AGAINST the table, close enough to touch it: the near edge of the table is cropped by the bottom edge of the canvas, so no trestle leg, no table underside and no patch of ground beneath the table is visible anywhere — the cloth runs off the bottom of the frame. Measuring downwards from the top edge of the canvas, THE FAR EDGE OF THE TABLE IS A HORIZONTAL LINE CROSSING THE WHOLE FRAME AT ABOUT 62 % OF THE WAY DOWN, and everything below that line down to the bottom edge is the bare cloth-covered table top, where the goods for sale will later be laid out in a row across the frame. Nothing rests on the cloth: no cash box, no tin, no basket, no object of any kind, and no part of the stallholder's body — no hand, no arm, no shoulder, no silhouette — appears anywhere in the picture. The viewer simply stands in the stallholder's place, unseen. The table must not be deep, must not stretch up towards the middle of the picture, and must never reach the centre of the canvas. Beyond its far edge the market street begins immediately, and the whole upper two thirds of the canvas belong to the street and to the space where a visitor will stand. Everything above that line, from 45 % up to the top of the canvas, is the far side of the market street, drawn in the same clean sepia ink line-art as the rest — crisp outlines, flat colour wash, every element still clearly legible, simply lighter in tone and smaller with distance: the striped canopies of two or three neighbouring stalls, plane-tree foliage, the pale façade of a building behind them. A shallow sliver of pavement runs just behind the table and the rest of the height is filled by those stalls and trees, so the eye reads a lively street rather than a bare surface. This whole upper zone stays clear of people: a visitor standing just behind the table will later be drawn there, framed from the waist up, filling most of the frame's width. The market beyond the table is BUSY AND ALIVE: the neighbouring stalls are dressed with wares — crates of books, stacked china, hanging frames, baskets, a lamp, a birdcage — and people are about their Sunday morning, shoppers strolling in twos and threes along the aisle, a stallholder leaning over their own goods, a child trailing behind an adult, a dog on a lead, a bicycle propped against a plane tree, bunting strung between two canopies. All this life belongs to the street in the upper part of the picture and to the stalls on either side; the aisle immediately behind our own table stays clear, so that a visitor can later step into it.
camera: The shot is one single continuous static frame: the composition holds exactly as it is in the input image, from the first frame to the last, as if the picture had simply come to life. Exactly ONE person is visible in the whole shot — the visitor described below — and she stays on the far side of the table throughout. Everything else that moves is the life of the market far behind her. Keep the exact same illustration style, palette, line quality and paper grain as the input image. Do not add text, captions, subtitles, logos or UI elements to the picture.
ambiance: Ambient sound bed, constant and identical throughout: the muffled hubbub of a Sunday neighbourhood flea market — distant chatter, footsteps on gravel, a bicycle bell far away, occasional clink of coins. Low, steady, no music, no sudden change in density or level.

episodes.acheteur: a French woman in her thirties, faded denim jacket, loose bun, round glasses, canvas tote bag on her shoulder, curious and friendly
episodes.fond: autumn morning, low raking light, two strollers passing in the distance
episodes.accroche: Elle vaut combien, à votre avis ?

plan1.action: she is holding the marine watercolour up in both hands, tilting it towards the light to read the signature
plan1.demande: Elle est signée, celle-là… vous en voulez combien ?
plan1.reaction: she blinks, her eyebrows shoot up and she lets out a small astonished breath — the price is far more than she expected

plan2.action: she lays the watercolour back down on the cloth, folds her arms and tilts her head with a half-smile
plan2.replique: Vingt-cinq, et je la prends tout de suite.
